pages.name: How to Use This Book
pages.subtitle: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
How to Use This Book

This book teaches Grade 6 learners to spell English words by understanding how sounds map to letters. Every unit follows the same pattern so that learners know what to expect and can work independently.

The Structure of Each Unit
  • Word Store — a short list of words that all follow one spelling pattern.
  • Key Ideas — the rule or pattern explained in plain language.
  • Word Sort — grouping words by sound or spelling.
  • Reading Passage — a short text that uses the target pattern naturally.
  • Word Meaning — matching words to definitions and completing sentences.
  • Proofreading — finding and correcting misspelled words.
  • Proving Task — writing original sentences using the Word Store.
For Teachers and Parents

Teach one unit per week. Begin by reading the Word Store aloud, then discuss the Key Ideas. Use the passages for guided reading and dictation. The Answer Key and Glossary at the back support independent study.

Key Ideas
  • A blend is two or three consonants whose sounds flow together: splash, strong, brush, plant, thread, cream, frost, glass, twist, stamp.
  • A digraph is two consonants that form one new sound: chick, thorn, whisper, shrimp, thank.
  • In blends, you hear every letter. In digraphs, the two letters make a single sound.

Key Ideas
  • The long /ū/ sound (like the name of the letter U) appears in words like uniform, useful, and value.
  • The spelling pattern can be a single u in an open syllable (u-ni-form), ue at the end (value, rescue), or ew (not in this list, but important to know).
  • Try to visualize each word as you spell it. The u sound is often very clear at the start of a syllable.

pages.name: Glossary
pages.subtitle: PHONICS TERMS
pages.html:
Glossary
TermMeaning
BlendTwo or three consonants whose sounds flow together (splash, strong).
ConsonantAny letter that is not a vowel.
DigraphTwo consonants that form one new sound (chin, ship, thin).
DiphthongTwo vowels that form a new sound (coin, owl).
Long vowelA vowel that says its own name (cake, feet, pie).
PhonemeThe smallest unit of sound in a word.
PhonicsTeaching reading by linking letters to sounds.
ProofreadTo read and correct errors in writing.
SchwaAn unstressed vowel sound, heard as a soft "uh".
Short vowelA vowel with a short sound (apple, egg, igloo).
Silent letterA letter that is written but not pronounced (knock, island).
SuffixA group of letters added to the end of a word (-ing, -ful, -ment).
SyllableA unit of sound in a word containing one vowel sound.
Word StoreThe list of spelling words for a unit.
